segments.text: - Hello, everyone,
welcome back to Altium Academy.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.

Today, we're going to be
testing and bringing up

our NFC Reader Board project
that we worked on a while ago.
It finally came back from manufacturing,

and I've got it frankensteined
here on the bench
and ready to test.
So, if you haven't seen our earlier videos
about this project,

make sure to check out the
links in the description,
you can go watch those videos.

And now, let's go ahead
and hop onto the bench,
and get started.
(upbeat music)
So we finally got this NFC reader board
back from manufacturing.
You can see the board right here.
And we had these boards
built through TapRen Technology Solutions.
And you may remember recently
from one of our podcast episodes,

we had Tristan Ren from
TapRen on the podcast

while we were at PCB
West on the show floor.

So they handled the
manufacturing for these boards,
and I'm really happy with the results.

And now we've got everything
set up here on the bench
so we can do some testing.
So here what I have on the bench

is I have the board
hooked up to my computer

so we can flash the
firmware onto the board,
make sure it all boots up,

and we have the board hooked
up to our power supply,

we've got our Rigol
power supply over here,

and we're going to then do
a little bit of load testing
on the main output rail.
So we have a 12-volt output rail

that needs to deliver some
power to a downstream device.

And then we also have a relay
here that we're going to test,

and we're going to make sure
that this relay triggers

once a logic signal is
applied to this relay.
Now what we're gonna do here is,
first, we'll do the load testing,
we'll do the relay test,
and then after that,

we'll make sure this thing will
flash and take the firmware,
and then we will boot it up,

we'll make sure it's going
through its main loop,
and then after that,
we're gonna hook up our NFC antenna

and make sure that it responds
to one of these NFC tags,
and then toggles the relay.
Now as you can see here,
we only have the board hooked up to power
and to the electronic load,

but there is some additional
equipment that we need
to do the RF testing.
And one of those things that we need
is one of these little RF tags.

So these RFID tags are ISO
14443-A compliant tags.

The design is gonna then sense
the presence of this tag,
and then once you push the button,
it'll pass power through that relay.
Now, you need an antenna for this design

in order to sense the
presence of that tag.
And so, for that,

we have a Mikroelektronika-4001
RFID/NFC Antenna.

And as you can see here, it
has a little U.FL connector
that you use to connect to this board.

So we have a little
right-angle U.FL connector
that is then gonna connect to this board,

and then when we bring
the RFID tag nearby,
it should sense its presence,
and then it'll toggle the relay.

Once we then push the
button, it then passes power,
and then everything should be good.
Now you can buy these RFID tags on Amazon,
you can buy them on Alibaba,
and you can even buy them on DigiKey,
for example,

you can get a Adafruit
Industries' 5459 RFID tag,
as you can see here on screen.
And if you just take a look at this image,

you can get a sense for
how large the coil is
inside this NFC tag.
And so, the size of that coil
is going to be the primary determinant
of the range, or the detection range,

that you'll get when
you're using this design.

Now there's also a power
output setting on the NFC chip
that's on this board,

and that power output can
be set in the firmware,
but if you put the power output too high,
you might kick this into an oscillation,

and it might fail to detect
one of these RFID tags.

So you need to test it with
some different power settings

in order to get just
the right power output.
But as you can see here,
this is an example of one of these tags
and what the coil inside looks like.
Now there are some other RFID tags
like that are in card format,
they're basically like credit card size,
and they have larger coils than this.

And you can probably get some
better detection distance
with one of those RFID tags

rather than using one of
these small keyfob tags.

So now, let's go ahead
and turn on the power,
make sure this thing doesn't catch on fire

and do a little bit of testing
before we flash the firmware.
Let's go ahead and get started.

As you can see, we got our
nice, bright green LED,
so we know the board has turned on.
And the first thing we can do

is just do some load
testing on the 12-volt rail.

So you can see, we've
got a 12-volt output,

which is great, that's
exactly what we wanted.

We can go ahead and start
ramping up the current.

Now we do have a three-amp
maximum current output
on our power supply,
so we do need to be mindful of that.
But let's go ahead and just ramp this up
to a little over an amp,

and see how far we can go
before this thing drops out.

So we're already up to
about one and a half amps,

which is great, that's a
good amount of power output.
And you can see here,

we get up to about
1.8-amps, so that's not bad.

So we're getting 1.8-amps
at 12-volts output,
so that's pretty good.

And you can see here, it
just kicks right back on
once we turn off the electronic load.

So not bad for our initial
test with load testing.

So the next thing that I
want to test is the relay.
And before I try to toggle the relay

with the firmware conditions
or anything like that,

I wanna just test that
we can do it directly

by applying the logic level
directly to the relay circuit.
So if you take a look at the schematics,

you'll be able to see what
the relay circuit looks like.

Here, I have a pin that
I have hooked up to,

or a probe, I should say,
that I have hooked up
to our power supply on the second rail.
And here we have our 12-volt output
that we're using to power the board,
and then here we have a 3.3-volt output
that we're gonna use to toggle the relay,

which basically simulates
one of our logic levels.
So once the relay toggles,
we should then get a short circuit

between these two terminals
on the multimeter.
So let's go ahead, turn on the board,

and you can see here,
it's powering up nicely.

And then, I'm gonna snake
my probe right through here,
we're gonna turn on the probe,
and you can see the probe is at 3.3 volts.

And let's go ahead and
tap the other side of R3,
and make sure this relay clicks on.

(multimeter beeping)
And there you go,
you can see that it's toggling on,
and the multimeter is shorting out.
So, here, let's go ahead and do it again.

(relay clicking)
(multimeter beeping)

And so, you can hear that
it makes an audible click,

whenever that relay turns
on, exactly as expected,
and then we're getting the short circuit

that we expect between these
terminals on the multimeter.

So if you wanna see how
that circuit completes
and how I tested it,
take a look at the schematics,
those are linked in the video description.

So this is good, we did some
load testing on the main rail,

and then we were also able to
show that the relay circuit
does work and toggle correctly.
And now what we wanna do is we wanna flash
all of the firmware onto this board.
So I have all of the firmware compiled,

but we're gonna do a
little bit of configuration
in the ESP32 IDF,

and then we're gonna go
through the flashing process
and make sure it all flashes.

Now one thing that I've
done in this design

is I've placed a little two-pin
header here with this wire.
And the reason I did that
was so that I don't have to sit there

and manually hold the reset
button the entire time
that this board is flashing.
Instead, I can just put this wire,
it shorts that connection to ground,
and then it's going to ensure

that it is held to ground
the entire time I'm flashing.
Then once the flashing is completed,

we just turn off the power,
disconnect this wire,
and then we're good to go,
and boot it up and see if it works.
So let's go ahead and jump here on screen.

Here, I have the ESP-IDF 5.0
open on the Command prompt.
And the first thing that we wanna do
is we wanna take a look at the menuconfig.

Now what I've done first is
I've gone over to the directory
with my project files,
we're gonna go into the menuconfig,

and we're gonna just check
a couple of things first
before we do the flashing.
So the first thing I wanna take a look at
is Component config,

and then I wanna take a look
at the ESP System Settings.
So first, I want to make sure
that the watchdog timer is disabled.
And as you can see here,

the Enable Watchdog Timer
option is unchecked,

so we know that the
watchdog timer is disabled.
And then I wanna make sure
that Interrupt watchdog is selected.
So watchdog timer

is essentially going to
continuously reset the system,
if there's a fault,

we want to just turn
that feature off for now
while we're doing this testing.

And, of course, you can then
go through, do your testing,

and then turn that back
on later if you need it.

Once that is done, make
sure to hit the Save button,
just click the S key,

and then it will save that
to your sdkconfig file.

So we're gonna go ahead
and exit out of this.
The next thing that we need to do is,
of course, build the firmware to a binary

that incorporates the options
that we set up in menuconfig.

To do that, we would just
use the idf.py build command,

and that is going to go
through and build your firmware
down to a binary.
So I've already done that.
You can see here right above this line
on the Command Prompt,

it says No changes to save
to the sdkconfig file,

so we don't need to
rebuild this as a binary.

So I'm just gonna use
the existing binary here
that I have for this firmware.
After that, you want to then go through

and make sure that you have
identified your COM port
for your connection to this ESP32 board.
And then you will use this command

that you see here on screen
to flash the firmware
onto the board.
So how do you identify the COM port?

If you're using Windows, you
can use the Device Manager.

What I will sometimes do
is just open up Tera Term,

because you can see here
when I open up Tera Term,
it's then going to show me
what is the COM port assigned
to my USB to UART interface board

that I'm using to connect
to my ESP32 board.
So these little USB to UART boards
that I use for these connections,
you can see I have one right here.

You can buy these on
Amazon for really cheap,

they sell 'em in like
three packs or five packs,
you know, if one ever breaks,
just grab the next one and keep rolling.
And I like to use these
to try and then flash all the firmware
onto the boards that I design.
So let's go ahead and put that away.

And then, here, we're gonna
exit out of Tera Term,

and then we're gonna use
the flash command here,
and we're gonna go through and flash it,
and we'll see what happens.
All right, so now you can see
that we've gotten to this point,
it is finished flashing.

We're just gonna go ahead and
hit Control + right bracket,
and then quit.
And that's it, we're done.

We have that firmware
flashed onto this device.
So now what we're gonna go ahead and do
is just power cycle it.

I'm gonna disconnect that
reset wire that I have here.
We'll turn this back on.
And you can see it boots back up again.

So now we have a different
LED flashing here.

We have our green LED
as well as our red LED.
And this red LED is one of our indicators

stating that we don't
have a RFID tag nearby.
And, of course, right now,
we don't even have the antenna hooked up,
so we'll get to that in just a moment.

But what I wanna do here
is bring up Tera Term,

we're gonna go ahead and turn
this off for just a moment,
and we're gonna set up our serial prompt.

So we're gonna set up
our serial prompt here
by selecting Serial.
We're gonna go in here to our Serial port.
We're gonna configure this at 115,200 BOD.
I'm gonna bring this up at full screen,

and let's start this
up and see what we get.
All right, so now you can see
that the device is in its main loop.
And essentially what it's trying to do
is it's trying to locate an RFID tag.

So it is reading the detection
results from the TRF NFC chip
that then feeds back over to the ESP32.

So this is great, it has
started up into our main loop.

You can see it's just
running in our main loop
exactly as we want it to,
and that's perfect.

So now what I'm gonna do is
I'm gonna go back on screen,
I'm gonna get our antenna and hook it up,
I'm gonna test it with our RFID tag,
and we're gonna make sure
that the firmware detects the RFID tag
and toggles correctly,
and then we'll go ahead and wrap this up.

All right, everybody, so
here I am in my home office,

and I had to go home to
get our micro E antenna.
And you can see right here on the desk,
there's the board,
it's hooked up to our USB to UART module.
And then you can see right here,

there is that little
micro E antenna module,

and we're all hooked up to
a small bench power supply.
So I have Tera Term on screen,

it's all hooked up and
ready to go with this board.
So let's go ahead and turn this bad boy on
and see what happens.

So you can see here it goes
through some initial messages,
and here you can see that it says

it's in the initial state
ready to detect an NFC tag.
So I'm gonna take my NFC tag right here,
you can see the coil and everything,

I'm gonna put that right
here next to the antenna,

and there you go, you
can see it changes state.
So now it's in its ready state.

Once I click on the button,
now we're in the run state.

So you probably can't
hear the relay switch
when that happens, but, hey, that's okay.
You can see now it's in the third state,
once we press that button,

this is all working
exactly as we want it to.

So when you go into the
source code for this firmware,
you can of course modify it to display
whatever messages you want.

Most of this messaging that
you're seeing on screen
is output from the TRF chip
that's being provided to the user
through the UART interface.
You can also do things such as toggle
whether or not the relay turns on or off,
so you have some control over that.
And essentially what this relay is doing

is just completing a circuit
when you click that button.
Thanks for watching this video everybody.

And, of course, if you are
interested in the project files
for this design,

make sure to check out the
links in the description,

you can download all of
those project files for free.

You'll also see a link to a
blog on the Altium website
that describes the project,

goes over some of the
engineering decisions,

and gives you everything
you need to know about NFC
with ISO 14443 part A and part B designs,
as well as the other ISO standards.

Once again, thanks for
watching, everybody,

make sure to hit that Like
button, hit the Subscribe button,

leave your comments and questions
in the Comments section,

and don't forget to call
your fabricator, folks.
We'll see you next time.
(enigmatic whooshing)

title: NFC Reader Testing: Flashing and Validating the Project
